\label{lesson:HI-C272-gali}



\begin{quote}

\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \hi{गली}}
\textbf{\hi{गली}} — \emph{galī} — \textquotedblleft{}a lane\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\hi{गली}} (\emph{galī}) is a tadbhava, a word inherited and reshaped by sound change. It comes from \emph{*galī}, \textquotedblleft{}defile, lane\textquotedblright{}, a form CDIAL reconstructs from its descendants (CDIAL 4085).
\end{cousinweb}

\section[\texorpdfstring{\hi{जुलूस} (jalūs)}{जुलूस (jalūs)}]{\hi{जुलूस} (jalūs) — a procession}

\label{lesson:HI-C272-jalus}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Hindi for a street corner, then the Hindi for a fair.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \hi{जुलूस}}
\textbf{\hi{जुलूस}} — \emph{jalūs} — \textquotedblleft{}a procession\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\hi{जुलूस}} (\emph{jalūs}) is a loan from Arabic \emph{julūs}, \textquotedblleft{}a sitting; enthronement\textquotedblright{}, which reached Hindi through Persian. Its Arabic root is \emph{j-l-s} (Lane). Hindi uses it for the procession that went with it.
\end{cousinweb}
